v.why: With edge 5 absent, removing the direct input-to-output edge leaves at most one path (via edge 4) to the output, so the drop is far larger (e.g. exp 43).
If edge 4 is absent, deleting edge 3 forces all signal through node 2, risking disconnection and much larger accuracy loss.
With edge 1 absent, cutting edge 0 kills both intermediate nodes, leaving only edge 3, so the penalty is much larger (exps 72, 100).
With edge 0 absent, edge 1 is the only feed into the intermediate nodes, so removing it collapses the cell to edge 3 alone.
Replacing a parameter-free pooling op on the first edge with a 3x3 conv adds much more capacity than replacing a skip (exps 9, 31, 35 vs 2, 67).
Avg-pooling on the input-output edge blurs the shortcut; swapping it for a conv gives large gains (exps 34, 48) versus small ones when replacing skip or 1x1 conv.
Replacing the clean identity shortcut with pooling destroys the residual path that stabilizes training (exps 8, 83).
Turning the last conv into the output node into pooling removes key learnable capacity (exps 18, 64), unlike replacing a skip (exp 39).
Replacing a conv on the final edge with identity loses capacity on the main path (exp 56), much more than replacing pooling or none.
Swapping a 3x3 conv on the input-output edge for identity removes capacity, whereas replacing none or pooling with skip adds a beneficial residual (exps 25, 75).

raw:
Each hypothesis below is grounded in the 100 measurements and in how the cell is wired:
- **Disconnection:** removing an edge that is the only route to the output has a catastrophic effect (experiments 43, 53, 100).
- **What the edit replaces:** turning a convolution into a pooling or skip op hurts much more than replacing a non-conv op. Swapping a pooling or skip op for a convolution helps more.
- **Overloaded cells:** cells dominated by skips or pooling gain the most from adding convolutions. Pruning a redundant skip can also help them (experiments 40, 57, 89, 91).
